questions.question: Which graph correctly represents the relationship between launch angle and time of flight for a projectile? (Take the launch-angle axis to span $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$.)
questions.answer: **B.** $T=\dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$, which rises to a maximum at $90^\circ$ and falls to zero at $180^\circ$. (The paper does not state the axis range; over $0^\circ$–$90^\circ$ only, none of the graphs would be right.)

questions.question: Using a homemade projectile launcher a student investigated projectile motion and found that the launcher did not produce a consistent initial velocity. The type of error this produced is best described as
questions.answer: **D.** The velocity varies unpredictably from launch to launch, scattering the results.

questions.question: The diagram shows a cyclist turning on a banked track. Which statement about the forces acting on the cyclist is correct?
options: All the forces are balanced, allowing him to travel at a constant speed.
The net force acting on the cyclist creates a centripetal force.
The force acting on the cyclist parallel to the bank is balanced by the centripetal force.
The component of the normal force perpendicular to the slope is equal to the weight force.
questions.answer: **B.** In circular motion the net force is not zero; it points to the centre and is the centripetal force.

questions.question: A class investigated centripetal force using the apparatus shown. A student found a graph of their results with unlabelled axes, also shown. Which pair of variables was most likely graphed?
questions.answer: **A.** $F=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $F$ against $v$ is a parabola through the origin.

questions.question: Thomson's charge-to-mass experiment
options: calculated the mass of the electron.
measured the charge of an electron.
provided evidence that cathode rays had mass.
supported Hertz's claims about cathode rays.
questions.answer: **C.** Measuring a charge-to-mass ratio showed that cathode rays are particles with mass. It did not give charge or mass separately.

questions.question: The rollercoaster trolley shown has a constant speed through the circular dip. Which description best analyses the forces acting on the trolley?
options: The normal force on the trolley is less than when travelling on a flat surface.
The centripetal force is equal to the normal force.
The sum of the normal force and the gravitational force is equal to the centripetal force.
None of the above are correct.
questions.answer: **C.** The vector sum $N+mg$ provides the upward centripetal force.

questions.question: Which pair of current-carrying conductors has the weakest force acting between them?
questions.answer: **B.** $F\propto\dfrac{I_1I_2l}{d}$. In units of $I^2l/r$: A $=2$, B $=\frac12$, C $=1$, D $=2$.

questions.question: The first graph shows the variation of flux through a generator coil over one revolution. Which graph (A–D) shows the corresponding EMF?
questions.answer: **A.** $\varepsilon=-\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$. The flux starts at a (negative) turning point and then increases, so the EMF starts at zero and goes negative.

questions.question: The first graph shows the variation of flux through a generator coil over one revolution. The diagrams show cross-sections of the coil in the field. Which position was the coil in at the start of the graph?
questions.answer: **B.** The flux has maximum magnitude at the start, so the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field.

questions.question: The main difference between a controlled and an uncontrolled nuclear chain reaction is
options: the number of neutrons released at each fission.
the amount of energy released in each fission.
the mass defect per fission is greater in uncontrolled reactions.
questions.answer: **D.** Controlled reactions absorb excess neutrons so that the fission rate stays steady.

questions.question: Which equation shows the correct decay of cobalt-60 to nickel-60?
questions.answer: **A.** Beta-minus decay raises the atomic number by one, emitting an electron and an antineutrino.

questions.question: A wire conductor XY is moving to the right (first diagram). Which magnetic field (A–D) must it pass through to induce a net positive charge at end Y?
questions.answer: **A.** Force on a positive charge is $q\vec v\times\vec B$. To push it towards Y with $v$ to the right, $B$ must be into the page.

questions.question: Foucault measured the speed of light by reflecting light off a rotating mirror to a fixed mirror and back; while the light travelled, the rotating mirror turned through a small angle. Using the angle and the mirror's angular velocity he calculated $c$. The smaller the angle, the greater the uncertainty. What is the easiest adjustment to increase the angle?
options: Increase the distance between the mirrors.
Decrease the distance between the mirrors.
Increase the rotational velocity of the rotating mirror.
Decrease the rotational velocity of the rotating mirror.
questions.answer: **C.** The angle is $\omega t$. Spinning the mirror faster is simpler than lengthening the light path.

questions.question: What energy is released by an electron–positron annihilation (both initially at rest)?
A polarised light source enters a polarising filter as shown. Which adjustment would produce the greatest reduction in light intensity?
questions.answer: **C.** By Malus' law, $I\propto\cos^2\theta$. The angle between the axes becomes: A $70^\circ$, B $10^\circ$, C $80^\circ$, D $10^\circ$. C is closest to $90^\circ$.

questions.question: Calculate the work function of copper, which has a threshold frequency of $1.0\times10^9$ MHz.
Which electron transition in a hydrogen atom would emit the shortest wavelength?
questions.answer: **C.** The largest energy drop (3rd to 1st level) gives the shortest wavelength. D is an absorption.

questions.question: What significant change to the atomic model did the Rutherford gold foil experiment lead to?
options: Electrons existed in energy shells surrounding the nucleus.
The nucleus was a positive space.
The atom is mostly empty space.
questions.answer: **D.** Most alpha particles passed straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space with a tiny dense nucleus.

questions.question: Calculate the wavelength of a 59.4 g tennis ball travelling at 170 km h$^{-1}$.
What wave phenomena are shown in the experiment in the diagram?
questions.answer: **B.** Waves spread out from each slit (diffraction) and overlap to form interference lines.

questions.question: Low Earth orbit satellites experience significant orbital decay, have a short life span and are difficult to monitor. Explain why they are still used extensively.
questions.answer: Their small orbital radius gives a short period, so they pass over the Earth's surface many times a day at close range, which is ideal for imaging, mapping and monitoring. They are also cheaper to launch (less energy needed) and give low signal delay.

questions.question: A car travels at constant speed and constant height on a frictionless track banked at $15^\circ$ with turning radius 26.0 m. The centripetal force on the car is 3040 N. Determine the mass of the car.
questions.answer:
$N\cos15^\circ=mg$ and $N\sin15^\circ=F_c$, so $F_c=mg\tan15^\circ$. $m=\dfrac{3040}{9.8\tan15^\circ}\approx1.16\times10^3$ kg.

(The school's working writes $\sin15^\circ$, although its value of 1158 kg comes from $\tan15^\circ$.)

questions.question: A 1158 kg car on a frictionless $15^\circ$ banked track of radius 26.0 m experiences a centripetal force of 3040 N. Determine the minimum coefficient of friction required for it to travel round an unbanked track of the same radius at half that speed.
questions.answer: $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{3040\times26}{1158}}=8.26$ m s$^{-1}$, so the new speed is 4.13 m s$^{-1}$. Friction supplies the centripetal force: $\mu mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $\mu=\dfrac{4.13^2}{26\times9.8}\approx0.067$.

questions.question: In terms of mechanical energy, explain why the work done on a satellite in a constant circular orbit around the Earth is zero.
questions.answer: Its speed is constant, so its kinetic energy is constant; its radius is constant, so its gravitational potential energy is constant. Work done equals the change in energy, which is zero (the gravitational force is always perpendicular to the motion).

questions.question: Explain why the mass of an object is not a factor in determining its escape velocity.
questions.answer: Escape velocity is the minimum launch speed for which the kinetic energy equals the energy needed to move to infinity: $\frac12mv^2=\dfrac{GMm}{r}$. The object's mass $m$ cancels, giving $v_{esc}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{r}}$, which depends only on the central body's mass and the starting distance.

questions.question: A plane flies at a constant altitude of 200.0 m and speed 300.0 m s$^{-1}$ when it fires a missile. The missile's engine accelerates it at 25.0 m s$^{-2}$ for 10.0 s in a straight line at the same altitude; it then follows projectile motion to hit a target on the ground. Calculate the distance travelled by the missile in the first 10 seconds.
questions.answer: $s=ut+\frac12at^2=300\times10+\frac12\times25\times10^2=4250$ m.

questions.question: A plane flies at a constant altitude of 200.0 m and speed 300.0 m s$^{-1}$ when it fires a missile. The missile's engine accelerates it at 25.0 m s$^{-2}$ for 10.0 s in a straight line at the same altitude; it then follows projectile motion to hit a target on the ground. The missile travels 4250 m during the powered stage. Determine the horizontal distance from the target at which it should be fired.
questions.answer: Speed after 10 s: $300+250=550$ m s$^{-1}$. Fall time: $200=4.9t^2$, $t=6.39$ s. Projectile range $=550\times6.39=3514$ m. Total $=4250+3514\approx7.76$ km.

questions.question: The Earth's average distance from the Sun is 1.00 AU and Saturn's is 9.00 AU. Calculate Saturn's period in Earth years.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{r^3}{T^2}$ is constant: $T^2=9^3$, so $T=27$ years.

questions.question: Justify Lenz's law.
questions.answer: Lenz's law: an induced EMF drives a current whose magnetic field opposes the change in flux that produced it. If instead the induced current reinforced the change, the flux would change even faster, inducing a larger current and so on, creating energy from nothing. Opposing the change means work must be done to produce the electrical energy, as required by conservation of energy.

questions.question: Identify the device shown in the diagram and explain how it works.
questions.answer: A step-down transformer (fewer turns on the secondary). Alternating current in the primary coil produces a continually changing magnetic flux, which the iron core directs through the secondary coil. By Faraday's law the changing flux induces an EMF in the secondary; since $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$ and $N_s<N_p$, the output voltage is lower.

questions.question: A power plant generates 150 MW for a town 20 km away. The transmission wires have a resistance of $0.01\ \Omega$ per km, and the voltage drop between the plant and the town is 50 V. Calculate the power loss between the plant and the town.

A power plant generates 150 MW for a town 20 km away. The transmission wires have a resistance of $0.01\ \Omega$ per km, and the voltage drop between the plant and the town is 50 V. The power loss is 12 500 W. Calculate the transmission voltage to the town.
questions.answer: $I=\dfrac{V_{drop}}{R}=250$ A. $V=\dfrac{P}{I}=\dfrac{150\times10^6}{250}=600$ kV.

questions.question: The diagram shows the cross-section of a square coil of side 12.00 cm with 8 turns carrying 3.00 A in a uniform magnetic field of $2.50\times10^4$ T. The plane of the coil is at $40^\circ$ to the field. Calculate the torque on the coil.
questions.answer: $\tau=nIAB\sin50^\circ$ ($50^\circ$ between the normal and the field) $=8\times3\times0.0144\times2.5\times10^4\times\sin50^\circ\approx6.62\times10^3$ N m.

questions.question: The diagram shows the cross-section of a square coil of side 12.00 cm with 8 turns carrying 3.00 A in a uniform magnetic field of $2.50\times10^4$ T. The plane of the coil is at $40^\circ$ to the field. Determine the change in flux if the coil rotates $30^\circ$ from the position shown, in the direction of the motor torque (clockwise).
questions.answer: The angle between the normal and the field goes from $50^\circ$ to $80^\circ$. Per turn, $\Delta\Phi=BA(\cos80^\circ-\cos50^\circ)=360(0.174-0.643)\approx-169$ Wb (flux linkage change $\approx-1.35\times10^3$ Wb).

questions.question: A square coil of side 12.00 cm with 8 turns rotates in a uniform magnetic field of $2.50\times10^4$ T as a generator. Calculate the rotation rate, in revolutions per minute, needed for a peak-to-peak output of 2400 V.
questions.answer:
Peak EMF $=1200$ V $=nBA\omega$, so $\omega=\dfrac{1200}{8\times2.5\times10^4\times0.0144}=0.417$ rad s$^{-1}$. Rate $=\dfrac{60\omega}{2\pi}\approx3.98$ rpm.

Note: the school gives 6.25 rpm by using the average EMF over a quarter turn, but the stated 2400 V is the peak-to-peak value, which requires $\varepsilon_{max}=nBA\omega$.

questions.question: Two parallel plates 1.00 cm apart are set up as shown, the upper plate at $+200$ V and the lower earthed. An electron is placed at rest exactly midway between them. Calculate the net force on the electron.
questions.answer: $E=\dfrac{V}{d}=2.0\times10^4$ V m$^{-1}$. $F=qE=3.20\times10^{-15}$ N upward (towards the positive plate). Its weight ($8.9\times10^{-30}$ N, downward) is negligible. (The school writes $qE+mg$; the weight actually opposes the electric force, though this does not affect the result.)

questions.question: Two parallel plates 1.00 cm apart are set up as shown, the upper plate at $+200$ V and the lower earthed. An electron is placed at rest exactly midway between them. The net force on it is $3.20\times10^{-15}$ N. Determine how long it takes to touch a plate.
questions.answer: $a=\dfrac{F}{m}=3.52\times10^{15}$ m s$^{-2}$ upward. $0.005=\frac12at^2$, so $t\approx1.7\times10^{-9}$ s (it hits the upper plate).

questions.question: Discuss the significance of Maxwell's contribution to the development of our current understanding of electromagnetism and of wireless communication.
questions.answer:
- Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism: building on Gauss, Faraday and Ampère, his equations showed that changing electric fields produce magnetic fields and vice versa.
- He predicted self-propagating electromagnetic waves, with oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel.
- He calculated their speed as about $3\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$, matching the measured speed of light, and concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave and that other wavelengths should exist.
- Hertz confirmed this after Maxwell's death, producing and detecting radio waves and showing that they reflect, refract, interfere and polarise.
- Wireless communication (radio, television, mobile phones, Wi-Fi, satellites) generates such waves with oscillating charges in antennas.

His work was therefore highly significant: it is the foundation of classical electromagnetism and made wireless technology possible, although practical systems depended on later experimenters and engineers.

questions.question: A spaceship pilot passing through a spaceport observes that it takes 2.00 s to pass through. A person at the spaceport records the ship taking 4.39 s. Determine the ship's speed as a percentage of the speed of light.
questions.answer: The pilot measures the proper time. $4.39=\dfrac{2.00}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$, so $\dfrac vc=\sqrt{1-\left(\dfrac{2.00}{4.39}\right)^2}=0.890$, i.e. 89.0% of $c$.

questions.question: Outline an experimental validation of time dilation.
questions.answer: Muons created in the upper atmosphere have a mean lifetime of about $2.2\ \mu$s, too short for most to reach the ground even near light speed. Far more are detected at sea level than classical physics predicts, because in the Earth's frame their lifetime is dilated by the Lorentz factor.

questions.question: We have two models of light: a classical one and a quantum one. Explain the need for two models of light.
Contrast the processes that produce absorption and emission spectra from stars.
questions.answer: Absorption: continuous radiation from the star passes through cooler outer gas; atoms absorb photons whose energies match transitions **to higher** energy levels, leaving dark lines on a continuous background. Emission: excited atoms in hot low-density gas have electrons dropping **to lower** levels, emitting photons with $hf=\Delta E$, giving bright lines on a dark background.

questions.question: Explain how the rotational velocity of a star can be deduced from its spectrum.
questions.answer:
As a star rotates, one edge moves towards the observer (its light is blueshifted) and the other moves away (redshifted). The light from the whole disc is combined, so each spectral line is **broadened**. The width of the broadening, compared with the rest wavelength, gives the line-of-sight rotational speed ($\Delta\lambda/\lambda\approx v/c$); faster rotation gives wider lines.

Note: the school's sample answer describes the overall red or blue shift, which measures the star's translational (radial) velocity, not its rotation.

questions.question:
In a photoelectric experiment the results were:

| Frequency ($\times10^{14}$ Hz) | 7.0 | 7.5 | 9.0 | 9.9 | 11 | 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $K_{max}$ ($\times10^{-19}$ J) | 0.8 | 1.2 | 2.2 | 3.5 | 3.5 | 4.2 |

Convert the maximum kinetic energy at 7.5, 9.0 and 11 $\times10^{14}$ Hz to electron volts.
questions.answer: Divide by $1.602\times10^{-19}$: 0.75 eV, 1.4 eV and 2.2 eV.

questions.question:
In a photoelectric experiment the results were:

| Frequency ($\times10^{14}$ Hz) | 7.0 | 7.5 | 9.0 | 9.9 | 11 | 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $K_{max}$ ($\times10^{-19}$ J) | 0.8 | 1.2 | 2.2 | 3.5 | 3.5 | 4.2 |

Draw a graph of the data with a line of best fit, scaled so that the gradient gives Planck's constant and the vertical intercept shows the work function.
questions.answer: Plot $K_{max}$ (vertical) against frequency, with axes extended to show the negative intercept (about $-3.9\times10^{-19}$ J).

questions.question:
In a photoelectric experiment the results were:

| Frequency ($\times10^{14}$ Hz) | 7.0 | 7.5 | 9.0 | 9.9 | 11 | 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $K_{max}$ ($\times10^{-19}$ J) | 0.8 | 1.2 | 2.2 | 3.5 | 3.5 | 4.2 |

Using a graph of the data, calculate Planck's constant.
questions.answer: The gradient of the line of best fit is about $\dfrac{0.69\times10^{-19}}{10^{14}}$, so $h\approx6.9\times10^{-34}$ J s.

questions.question:
In a photoelectric experiment the results were:

| Frequency ($\times10^{14}$ Hz) | 7.0 | 7.5 | 9.0 | 9.9 | 11 | 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $K_{max}$ ($\times10^{-19}$ J) | 0.8 | 1.2 | 2.2 | 3.5 | 3.5 | 4.2 |

Using a graph of the data, determine the threshold frequency.
questions.answer: The line of best fit meets the frequency axis at about $5.7\times10^{14}$ Hz.

questions.question: Explain how the emission spectrum of hydrogen provided evidence for Bohr's model of the atom, with reference to one of his postulates.
questions.answer: Bohr postulated that an electron moving between stationary states emits or absorbs a photon with $hf=E_i-E_f$. Hydrogen emits only particular discrete wavelengths, as expected if only certain energy levels exist; the wavelengths match the differences between Bohr's calculated levels.

questions.question: Calculate the second longest wavelength in the Balmer series of hydrogen.
questions.answer: This is the $n=4\to2$ transition: $\dfrac1\lambda=1.097\times10^7\left(\dfrac1{4}-\dfrac1{16}\right)$, so $\lambda=4.86\times10^{-7}$ m.

questions.question: A sample of iodine-131, half-life 8 days, contains $1.2\times10^{13}$ nuclei. Calculate the decay constant.
A sample of iodine-131, half-life 8 days, contains $1.2\times10^{13}$ nuclei. Determine how many iodine-131 nuclei remain after 76 days.
questions.answer: $N=1.2\times10^{13}\times2^{-76/8}\approx1.7\times10^{10}$. (The school gets $1.6\times10^{10}$ because it rounds $\lambda$ to 0.087 before using it.)

questions.question: Compare the composition of a proton and a neutron in the Standard Model.
questions.answer: Both are baryons made of three first-generation quarks held together by gluons. A proton is two up and one down quark (uud, charge $+1$); a neutron is one up and two down (udd, charge 0).
